clue.text: This is curious — odds on proud being involved in deception, not I

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters of the word curious are the ones taken
the tangled letters go inside the trickery word, signalled by in
not I tells us to drop the letter I from the trickery word

parts.note: a swizzle is a swindle or con, British slang
the letter I as printed

indicators.note: letters that are involved are tangled up, so the word proud is jumbled

explanation.surface: A puzzled remark about a proud person caught up in some trickery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odds' takes the odd letters of curious; 'not' drops I from a swindle word to leave SWZZLE; 'being involved' jumbles proud and 'in' sets it inside. 'This' points at the very thing being solved.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-referential: the solver is holding the very object the word This points to, a grid of clued words.

clue.text: Wrong half of Hellas in Greek given to 23

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the word for Greek

parts.note: Attic is the Greek dialect of Athens, so it can mean Greek

indicators.note: wrong signals that those letters are set out in the wrong order
only the front half of the word Hellas is used, its first three letters

explanation.surface: Something about the wrong part of Greece being in a Greek setting, tied to sport.
explanation.walkthrough: Attic was the Greek dialect of Athens. 'Wrong' scrambles the front half taken by 'half of', and 'in' places it inside. 23 refers to 23-down, so 'given to 23' means keen on sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sporty or fond of physical games is described with this adjective; 23-down supplies the sense of sport.

clue.text: See 20
Extremely insensitive heart under building?

parts.note: hard means unfeeling or callous, extremely so
the core of something is its heart or centre

explanation.surface: A thoroughly callous heart lying beneath some structure.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the heart sits under the insensitive part, but 'under building?' is the definition: the question mark flags that the material is what goes beneath a building.
explanation.definitionFit: This rubble of broken brick and stone is laid as a foundation layer beneath roads and buildings.

clue.text: Iron wheel with new base

indicators.note: a new bottom letter replaces the old one: in a down entry the base is the last letter

parts.note: a Ferris wheel is the big fairground wheel
C, cytosine, is one of the bases in DNA

explanation.surface: An iron wheel fitted with a new base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with new base' swaps the bottom letter of FERRIS: S goes and C, a DNA base, comes in. 'Iron' looks like a noun but the definition is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes something containing or relating to iron, especially in its trivalent chemical state.

clue.text: Decoration for building to get reduction on the exterior

indicators.note: the cutting-down word lies on the outside, wrapped round the other piece

parts.note: paring is cutting down or trimming away
taken as written

explanation.surface: Builders aiming to get a discount on outside work.
explanation.walkthrough: Pargeting is ornamental plasterwork on the outside of houses, common in eastern England; 'on the exterior' wraps the trimming word round the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: This is decorative raised or patterned plaster applied to exterior walls, an ornament for a building.

clue.text: Which church has cover?

parts.note: that can stand for which as a relative pronoun

explanation.surface: A question about which church is insured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover' reads as insurance, but it means a roof covering of straw or reeds.
explanation.definitionFit: A roof of straw or reeds is a covering laid over a building.

clue.text: Compounding regal 4, flattery is our biggest fault

indicators.note: compounding means mixing together, so the letters are combined anew

parts.note: taken as written
4 in Roman numerals is IV
taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that adding regal flattery is our greatest failing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compounding' mixes REGAL, IV (4 in Roman numerals) and FLATTERY. 'fault' looks moral but is geological, and 'our' means the planet's.
explanation.definitionFit: This East African rift system is the largest geological fault zone on Earth, the world's biggest crack.

clue.text: Terrorists first and subsequently to get back … their own

definitions.text: Terrorists first and subsequently to get back … their own

parts.words: Terrorists first and subsequently to get back … their own
parts.note: after terrorists strike first, their victims then get their own back by hitting in return

explanation.surface: A grim account of a cycle of attack and revenge.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis splits the idiom 'get their own back', meaning take revenge; the clue describes the response that follows a first strike.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting one's own back after an attack is striking in return, taking revenge in kind.

clue.text: Jane's tribe on stage, with A for Antony?

explanation.surface: An actress's family appearing on stage, with Antony's initial.
explanation.walkthrough: Jane Asher is an English actress; Asher is one of the twelve tribes of Israel. 'on stage, with A for Antony' adds a third hint: A followed by the actor Antony Sher's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Asher bears the surname, and Asher, a son of Jacob, gave his name to an Israelite tribe.

clue.text: Married with no children, not being licensed

parts.note: s.p., sine prole, is the genealogical abbreviation for without issue

indicators.note: not tells us to remove the philosophical being from the word licensed

parts.note: ens is the philosopher's Latin word for being or existence

explanation.surface: A childless married couple, without any licence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes ENS from licensed, leaving LICED. Married is slang: being spliced means getting hitched.
explanation.definitionFit: Spliced is informal slang for wed, from joining two ropes together.

clue.text: A target set for aquatic event

indicators.note: set means arranged or placed, so the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A target being set up for a water sports competition.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat-racing meeting is an event held on water.

clue.text: Engineer's spoken question?

indicators.note: spoken means the word is heard, not seen written

parts.note: what is a typical question word

explanation.surface: An engineer's query, said out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: James Watt was the Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine.
explanation.definitionFit: James Watt, the Scottish inventor of the improved steam engine, is a famous engineer.

clue.text: Fellow sentinel keeps clubs for protection of train

parts.note: co- is the prefix for a fellow, as in co-worker

indicators.note: keeps means holds inside, so the club letter goes within the sentry word

parts.note: a sentinel is a watcher or guard
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: A guardsman friend carrying clubs to protect a railway train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps' puts C inside WATCHER after its W.
explanation.definitionFit: A metal frame on the front of a locomotive clears obstacles off the track, protecting the train.

clue.text: Game, not a good one, among poets

indicators.note: among means placed in the midst of the poets

parts.note: bards are poets
ill means bad, not good
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A poor game played among a group of poets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' tucks the bad-plus-one pieces inside the poets; 'not a good one' splits into two pieces, not a single idea.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue sport played on a cloth-covered table with three balls is one kind of game.

clue.text: Take course to be at ease

parts.note: rec., from Latin recipe, is the abbreviation for take on old prescriptions
a line is a course or path

explanation.surface: Advice to take a course in order to relax.
explanation.walkthrough: Recipe is Latin for 'take', printed at the head of prescriptions.
explanation.definitionFit: To lean back and rest is to be relaxed and comfortable.

clue.text: Wizard with access to standard return

indicators.note: the joining word gains access to the flag, going inside it
return means the flag word is read backwards

parts.note: a standard is a flag
and can mean with, together with

explanation.surface: A wizard gaining entry to a returning banner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns the standard backwards and 'access to' lets the joining word inside it. Gandalf is the wizard of The Lord of the Rings.
explanation.definitionFit: Gandalf is the famous wizard in Tolkien's Lord of the Rings books.

clue.text: Cooker for idiot to put in cooked vegetables

indicators.note: put in means the fool and the little word go inside the jumbled letters
cooked means messed about, so the short vegetable word is rearranged

parts.note: veg is short for vegetables
an ass is a fool
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe telling an idiot to add cooked vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' reads as a kitchen word in the surface but is the anagram signal on the short vegetable word; 'put in' sets the fool and the little word inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen appliance burning fuel gas for heating food is one kind of cooker.

clue.text: Unholy verse by the poet Lewis towards the end of April

indicators.note: unholy means without the saint, so ST is taken away

parts.note: a stanza is a verse of a poem
C. Day Lewis was a British poet laureate

explanation.surface: An irreverent poem by the poet Lewis, written late in April.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unholy' drops ST (saint) from STANZA, leaving ANZA. Anzac Day, 25 April, remembers Australian and New Zealand troops at Gallipoli.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian and New Zealand memorial day falls on 25 April, near the month's close.

clue.text: Building cover for recession initiated during infatuation

indicators.note: during means placed within the infatuation word

parts.note: a pash is a schoolchild's crush, British slang
an ebb is a falling back or recession
led means started or initiated

explanation.surface: Something about a building's cladding, a downturn, and a crush.
explanation.walkthrough: Pash is British schoolchild slang for a crush; 'during' sets the two short pieces inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pebbledash is a mortar render with small stones embedded, used as an exterior wall coating.

clue.text: Wind brake in building?

parts.note: a breeze is a light wind
a block is a brake shoe pressed on a wheel

explanation.surface: A gust of wind braking against a building.
explanation.walkthrough: A breeze block is a lightweight building block made with cinders.
explanation.definitionFit: This cinder block is a standard unit used in construction, a building material.

clue.text: Gather from leader in European countries

parts.note: de is French for from
duce is Italian for leader, as in Mussolini's title

explanation.surface: Learning something from a leader in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in European countries' tells us both pieces are foreign: DE from French, DUCE from Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather in the sense of conclude or infer is to reason something out.

clue.text: A 0.3125 lb return from sea

indicators.note: return means the weight letters are read backwards

parts.note: 0.3125 lb is five ounces, V for five plus OZ

explanation.surface: A small weight of fish returned from the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 0.3125 pounds is 5 ounces: V (Roman five) and OZ, turned round by 'return'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sea of Azov is an inland sea north of the Black Sea.

clue.text: Not the 25 play?

explanation.surface: A question whether a game is unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: 25 refers to 25-across, typical. A sport in biology is an organism that differs abnormally from its type.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutant departing from the norm is one sense; to sport is also to play or frolic.

clue.text: Oxymoronic region where letter has dash in it

indicators.note: in it means the flair word is put inside the letter

parts.note: zed is the British name for the letter Z
elan is dash or flair

explanation.surface: A self-contradictory place where a letter has a dash in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Zeeland, a Dutch province, sounds like sea-land, a contradiction in terms, as the land is reclaimed from the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch province's name means sea-land, a self-contradiction, making it an oxymoronic region.

clue.text: Extract from clay pit to be expected

indicators.note: an extract is drawn out and reworked, so the letters of clay pit are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something drawn out of a clay pit is unsurprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extract from' looks like a hidden-word signal, but no run of clay pit gives the answer; the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Something characteristic or normal is what one would expect.

clue.text: Was idle student introduced to Sunday's 1?

parts.note: L is a learner or student, as on L-plates
Azed is the Observer's Sunday crossword; 1 refers to 1-down

explanation.surface: A student slacking off with a Sunday puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 refers to 1-down; Azed is the setter of the Observer's Sunday crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: To laze is to idle or lounge about doing nothing.

clue.text: Disc containing extra drink for Bible translator in Yorkshire

indicators.note: containing means the disc letters hold the extra word inside

parts.note: CD is a compact disc
over means extra, left over
ale is a drink

explanation.surface: A record with a bonus drink for a Yorkshire Bible scholar.
explanation.walkthrough: Miles Coverdale, born in Yorkshire, made the first complete printed English Bible; Coverdale is also a Yorkshire dale.
explanation.definitionFit: Miles Coverdale translated the Bible into English, and the name is also a Yorkshire valley.
